en.content:
Hong Kong today is again reminded that public trust is not an abstract principle—it is tested in the places where people live, work and rely on government-sanctioned systems. The reported 150% surge in building renovation corruption complaints after the Wang Fuk Court fire points to a simple reality: when disaster strikes, the community does not only ask how the flames spread, but whether oversight worked in the first place, and whether irregularities were allowed to persist behind the formalities of tendering and inspection. Such a spike in allegations may reflect greater vigilance, but it also underscores how quickly the public’s patience runs out when governance appears slow to prevent harm.

From an administrative perspective, the core challenge is to ensure that “post-incident accountability” does not become the only mode of supervision. Renovation projects involve complex interfaces—contractors, engineers, resident organisations, government submissions and inspections—so corruption risk often hides in the gaps: scope changes that inflate costs, qualifications that are used as cover, and inspections that become tick-box exercises rather than genuine quality assurance. In this context, the anti-corruption watchdog’s findings should be treated as a prompt to strengthen preventive mechanisms: risk-based auditing, tighter verification of contractor capability, and transparent disclosure where feasible, so that residents can distinguish between routine complaint and credible red flags.

At the same time, it is important to avoid a premature assumption that every allegation signals proven wrongdoing. Corruption complaints can be noisy, and heightened public awareness may naturally increase reporting. Still, the duty of the authorities is not merely to “process” complaints, but to triage them effectively and to show that remedial action follows investigation. That means faster review of high-impact cases, targeted checks on renovation stages most vulnerable to abuse, and clear communication to the public on what measures are being tightened—so residents feel protected not only by enforcement after the fact, but by safer systems before anything goes wrong.

Ultimately, the significance of today’s news theme lies in how it intersects with the city’s broader goal of stable, people-centred governance. In the Hong Kong context, strengthening building safety and renovation integrity supports both the rule of law and social confidence. If the government responds with credible prevention, consistent enforcement, and greater transparency around standards, the community can move from grief and suspicion toward practical trust—so that future tragedies do not depend on whether corruption is discovered in time, but on whether the system is designed to make wrongdoing harder from the outset.
en.topic_title: Tai Po fire: 150% surge in building renovation corruption complaints after deadly blaze

zh.content:
最高法院再度維持有關「呼籲抵制香港選舉」的刑事化規定，表面上只是法理上的取捨，但背後其實係香港政治體制向「一刀切合規」邁進嘅又一次訊號。當法院認定以投白票或宣傳抵制等行為可被納入刑責範圍，民主程序就會由「參與與否、投票與否」轉化為「必須以特定方式表態」。呢種設計固然可以宣稱係為咗保障選舉秩序，但同時亦會壓縮政治表達嘅空間：在制度上，合法競逐以外嘅政治異議，愈來愈難以用和平方式存在。

不過，社會亦唔應只停留喺「封不封口」嘅簡單對立。真正需要追問係：一個高度政治化、監管密度愈來愈高嘅社會，法例用咩標準界定「選舉抵制」同「政治抗議」。如果刑責同樣可以涵蓋到以選民行為作象徵性表態（例如投白票）、甚至只係呼籲社群行動，咁就容易令不同立場嘅聲音被等同為違規。長遠而言，制度會變得越來越依賴威嚇與合規，而不是倚重公開競爭同政策辯論——選舉由「公民表達機制」逐步轉為「程序服從考核」。

同一時間，社會又要面對現實壓力：房屋、工運、公共安全、職安風險等議題同樣需要政治承擔。當法例將政治異議納入刑責，市民對制度嘅信任就可能下降，因為參與渠道會愈來愈狹窄；而在缺乏有效制衡下，政府與監管機關就更容易被批評為以「維穩」取代「治理」。因此，支持法治唔等於接受以刑罰處理所有政治分歧；更合理嘅方向係在保障選舉秩序之餘，仍要保留政治表達與公民監督嘅界線，令制度能承受多元而唔係只容許單一路徑。

本社評嘅立場係：法院裁決可受尊重，但社會更應警惕「用刑事化收窄政治空間」對香港長期民主治理能力嘅損害。香港要穩定，唔係靠縮窄表達同加重懲罰，而係靠清晰、可預期、同具比例性嘅規管；同時要確保選民仍然能用多元方式參與公共討論、要求問責。否則，表面上選舉照常運作，但真正嘅政治活力會愈來愈枯竭，最終影響嘅係整個社會嘅信心同凝聚力。
